title: Pruning
sub: Word Search, Combination Sum, N-Queens: mark and restore, sort and break, check a conflict in O(1)
cards/0/title: Word Search: a path where no cell is used twice
cards/0/body:
Word Search (LeetCode #79). Given an m × n grid of letters (up to 6 × 6) and a word of up to 15 letters, can you spell the word by moving between cells that share a side, never using a cell twice?

The signals of backtracking: we look for a path, every step has a choice (up to four neighbours), and there is a constraint that depends on the path walked so far — “the cell is not taken”. That is why flood fill doesn’t fit: there a cell is marked forever, while here a cell that failed one path may be needed by another.

The key word of this lesson is pruning: cut a branch of the decision tree as soon as it is clear there is no answer in it. Good pruning doesn’t change the worst-case complexity, but it removes almost the whole tree on real data. Here the pruning is the very first wrong letter: on the word “ABCCED” we don’t continue the path “AB…” from the cell “F”.
cards/1/body:
From every cell we start Dfs(r, c, i): “can the word be finished from letter i, standing at (r, c)”. Cheap checks come first — out of the grid and the wrong letter: that is the pruning. If the letter fits, we mark the cell (write '#' right into the board — that letter never appears in a word), go to the four neighbours with i + 1, and restore the letter.

Invariant: exactly the cells of the current path from the start are marked. Restoring the letter is the same undo as path.RemoveAt in subsets: after the call returns, the board is the same as before it.

|| between the calls is evaluated lazily: as soon as one neighbour returns true, the rest are not touched — an early exit.

Cost: m·n starts, the first step has up to 4 neighbours, later up to 3 (the cell we came from is marked). The worst case is O(m·n·3ᴸ), where L is the word length; for 6 × 6 and L = 15 that is up to 7·10⁸, but only on nasty boards like “all letters A, word AAA…AB”. Memory is the recursion depth L.
cards/2/q: In Word Search the line board[r][c] = saved was forgotten. What breaks?
cards/2/options/0: Cells of a failed path stay '#', and another path that needs them can’t take them: false is possible when the word exists
cards/2/options/1: One cell can enter a path twice, and the code finds words that aren’t on the board
cards/2/options/2: Nothing: a failed path leads nowhere anyway, its cells are no longer needed
cards/2/options/3: The code crashes with IndexOutOfRangeException on the '#' character
cards/2/explain: The mark is only needed while the current path lasts. Without the restore, a cell that a dead-end path went through is “taken” forever — but from another start or in another order it may be needed. The answer becomes a false negative: the word is there, and the code says false.
cards/2/wrong/1: There is no double use: '#' matches no letter. The bug goes the other way — fewer cells are available than there should be.
cards/2/wrong/2: A dead-end path leads nowhere from this point and in this order. Its cells one by one can still belong to another, successful path.
cards/2/wrong/3: '#' is an ordinary character, the comparison board[r][c] != word[i] simply returns false. No index leaves the board.
cards/3/task: The same board, the word ECCB. The first E leads to a dead end, the second to the answer, and it will need the same C cells. Neighbours are tried in the order down, up, right, left; the rig doesn’t show marked cells or cells off the board. It will stop twice and ask what happens next.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Unmark (1,2) and return to (0,2) for its other neighbours
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Return false right away: the path from this E failed
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Take (0,2) again: it is a neighbouring C
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: Path E(0,3) → C(0,2) → C(1,2). A B is needed, but the neighbours of (1,2) are E, S, F and the marked (0,2). What does the code do?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: All four calls from (1,2) returned false, and the code restores the letter: board[1][2] = 'C'. The call returns to (0,2), which tries its remaining neighbours — to the left (0,1), a B, while a C is needed. (0,2) can’t be taken a second time: it is on the current path and marked.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: (1,2) = “C” fits: it was unmarked on the way back
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: (1,2) is skipped: the first path already used it
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: The search ends: a cell can be taken once in the whole search
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: A new start — E(2,2). Its neighbour above is (1,2) = C, which the first, dead-end path used. What will the rig show?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: A mark lives while the cell is on the current path. The first path was undone completely, and the board is clean again — so (1,2) and then (0,2) fit again, and to the left of (0,2) lies a B. Without restoring letters this would be a false negative.
cards/4/title: Combination Sum: start, and break after sorting
cards/4/body:
Combination Sum (LeetCode #39). Distinct candidates from 2 to 40, a target up to 40. Return all distinct sets that sum to target; a number may be used any number of times. For [2, 3, 6, 7] and 7 that is [2, 2, 3] and [7].

No duplicate sets. [2, 2, 3] and [3, 2, 2] are one set. As with subsets built by a loop, we pass start down: from here on we only take candidates with index ≥ i. A set is always built in non-decreasing order — so each one comes out exactly once. The difference from subsets: we recurse into Dfs(i, …), not i + 1, because the same number may be taken again.

Pruning. Sort the candidates. If candidates[i] > remain, every candidate to the right is larger than the remainder too — so not continue but break: we cut the whole tail of the loop. Without sorting you can’t do that — you’d have to check each one.

Cost: the depth is up to target / min, the branching up to k candidates; roughly O(k^(T/min)). Nobody expects an exact bound here; say “exponential, bounded by the number of answers, and pruning cuts almost everything”.
cards/5/task: Walk the Combination Sum tree for [2, 3, 6, 7] and target = 7: the nodes show the remainder. The rig will stop twice and ask what the loop does: answer from start and the sorting.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Take 2: remainder −1, the call comes back empty
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: path = [2, 2, 2], 1 left. What does the loop do?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: The smallest candidate, 2, is already larger than the remainder 1. The array is sorted, so 3, 6 and 7 won’t fit either — break ends the whole loop with one comparison. The code never enters the pruned branch at all.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: path = [3], 4 left. What is the next path?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: The 3 was taken at index 1, and the recursion went into Dfs(1, 4): the loop starts at the 3 itself, the 2 is to the left and is no longer considered. Otherwise [3, 2, 2] would appear — the same set as the [2, 2, 3] already found. Then 3 > 1 — break.
cards/6/q: Combination Sum on [2, 3, 6, 7], target = 7 returns [2, 2, 3], [2, 3, 2], [3, 2, 2], [7]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: The recursion gets start = 0: at every level the loop starts from the 2 again, and one set is built in every order — those are permutations, not combinations. It needs Dfs(i, …): from here on only candidates with an index no smaller than the current one. Dfs(i + 1, …) would forbid repeating a number and lose [2, 2, 3].
cards/7/body:
N-Queens (LeetCode #51), n ≤ 9. Place n queens on an n × n board so that no two attack each other, and return all placements. For n = 4 there are 2, for n = 8 — 92.

The first pruning is in the formulation: every row holds exactly one queen, so we decide row by row: at level r we pick a column. Instead of n² cells per level there are n options, and “two in one row” is impossible by construction.

The second is checking a conflict in O(1) rather than by scanning the placed queens. A queen at (r, c) occupies column c, the “↘” diagonal, along which r − c is constant, and the “↙” diagonal, along which r + c is constant. We keep three flag arrays: cols[c], diag[r + c] and anti[r − c + n] (shifted by n so the index is never negative). Place — three flags to true, take back — to false.

Cost: without pruning there are nⁿ options, with “one per row and column” at most n!, and the diagonals cut even more: for n = 8 the code visits 2 057 nodes, while the tree “one queen per row and column” would have 8! = 40 320 leaves alone.
cards/7/flow/0: Place(r): r == n → a placement is ready
cards/7/flow/1: for c: cols[c] or diag[r + c] or anti[r − c + n] → skip
cards/8/q: Build the loop that places a queen in row r.
cards/8/explain: The diagonals are checked by the same indices they are marked with: r + c and r − c + n. Without the shift, r − c goes negative as early as (0, 1) — IndexOutOfRangeException. Place — flags to true, take back after the recursion — to false. The next level is the next row, r + 1.
cards/9/task: Walk the placement of 4 queens: row by row, columns left to right, backtracking at a dead end. The rig will ask what to do when a row has no free cells left.
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Remove the queen from (1,2) and try (1,3)
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Remove the queen from (0,0) and start from (0,1)
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Put a queen on (2,3): it has the fewest threats
cards/9/goal/asks/0/q: Queens at (0,0) and (1,2). In row 2 all four cells are attacked. What does the code do?
cards/9/goal/asks/0/explain: The loop of row 2 ended without placing anything, and Place(2) simply returns. Control is back in the loop of row 1, right after the recursion: it clears the flags of the queen at (1,2) and takes the next column, 3. Backtracking goes one level up, not to the start: the choice in row 0 may still work with a different choice in row 1.
cards/10/title: Variations and where this shows up in games
cards/10/body:
Combination Sum II (#40): each candidate once, but the input has duplicates. Recurse into Dfs(i + 1, …), and equal neighbours on one level are skipped: i > start && c[i] == c[i − 1] — the same trick as in Subsets II.

Generate Parentheses (#22): all valid bracket strings of n pairs. The pruning is in the rules of choice: “(” is allowed while fewer than n are open, “)” while fewer are closed than open. Invalid strings are never built at all.

Faster Word Search. Two prunings before any search: count the letters of the board and of the word — if some letter is missing, return false at once; if the word’s first letter is more common on the board than its last, search for the reversed word — fewer starts.

Word Search II (#212): many words on one board. Running a search per word is expensive; the words go into a prefix tree, and one walk from each cell follows the tree directly — a branch ends when no word has that prefix (prefix trees are in the last unit).

Sudoku Solver (#37): try digits 1–9 in an empty cell, check the conflict with row, column and box flags — just like the queens.

In a game: checking that a generated puzzle level is solvable; finding words on a letter grid in a word game; placing objects under constraints like “not closer than”, “not on one line”. Pruning decides everything here: without it the search doesn’t fit even into a level load.
cards/10/deep:
Queens on masks. The code on the card stores what is taken not in three arrays but in three numbers. cols is the taken columns. d1 and d2 are the cells of the current row attacked by diagonals from above: moving one row down, a “↘” diagonal shifts one column right and a “↙” one column left, hence << 1 and >> 1. ~(…) inverts the bits, & full keeps the low n — we get every free column of the row in one expression. free & -free isolates the lowest set bit (in two’s complement -x is ~x + 1). An iteration is a few cycles, with no arrays and no per-column checks; this is the classic fast variant of the n-queens search.

Word Search: why reversing helps. On an “all A” board and the word “AAA…AB”, every start builds a huge tree of A’s and is cut only at the last letter. The reversed word “BAA…A” starts with the rare B: a handful of starts, and counting letters up front rejects a board without a B entirely. On nasty boards this is orders of magnitude faster — interviewers love it as a follow-up.

Sudoku and the choice heuristic. The order in which cells are filled matters more than how fast the check is. Take the cell with the fewest allowed digits (minimum remaining values): mistakes surface at the top levels of the tree, where pruning cuts more. Stronger still is constraint propagation: having placed a digit, strike it from the neighbours right away and detect a cell with zero options before recursing.

Unity. Level solvability checks run in the editor or at generation time, not in a frame. If the search does run at runtime, give it a node budget per frame and continue in the next one (a coroutine, an explicit stack instead of recursion), or move it into a Job: flags and masks are unmanaged and can be passed to Burst. Keep the board in a flat array and change it in place with restore — no state copies at every node.
cards/11/q: You are solving Word Search out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: neighbours by side only? may the board be modified? board and word sizes
cards/11/items/1: Say why it isn’t flood fill: whether a cell is taken depends on the current path
cards/11/items/2: Idea: DFS from every cell, mark the cell, go to the neighbours, restore the letter
cards/11/items/3: Write the code: bounds and letter checks first — that is the pruning — then the mark and the undo
cards/11/items/4: Run a word where the first path hits a dead end — check that the undo gives the cells back
cards/11/items/5: Complexity: O(m·n·3ᴸ) in the worst case, memory — depth L
cards/11/items/6: Suggest speedups: count letters up front and search from the rarer end
cards/11/explain: First agree on adjacency and on whether the board may be modified: that decides between writing '#' and keeping a separate array. A run with a dead end is the best test of the undo. Speedups at the end show that you think about pruning, not just the template.
cards/12/q: Match each problem with the pruning that makes it fast.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: Sort, and break when a candidate exceeds the remainder
cards/12/pairs/1/1: Stop at the first letter that doesn’t match
cards/12/pairs/2/1: Flags for the column and both diagonals
cards/12/pairs/3/1: “)” only while fewer are closed than open
cards/12/pairs/4/1: Skip an equal neighbour on the same level
